data.title: Door Hardware Bypass
data.summary: Controlled doors were opened without a credential by manipulating the hardware: slipping the latch, reaching the inside handle through a gap, or triggering the request-to-exit sensor from outside. The access control system recorded a normal exit or nothing at all.
data.description:
Electronic access control secures the decision to unlock, not the door. The common bypasses target the mechanism underneath it and are performed in seconds with improvised tools.

A spring latch with no deadlocking feature can be slipped with a shim. A gap under or beside the door admits a tool that reaches the interior handle or a push bar. Most effective of all is the request-to-exit sensor: a motion detector mounted inside, which releases the door for anyone leaving — and which can be triggered from outside through the door gap, releasing the lock and logging a legitimate exit.

None of these attacks leave an obvious trace, which means the compromise is both easy and unlikely to be investigated.
data.recommendation:
* Fit deadlatching hardware, and close gaps around door edges with astragals or latch guards.
* Replace motion-based request-to-exit with a push bar or sensor positioned so it cannot be triggered through the door, and alarm doors that open without a corresponding badge event.
* Fit door position sensors and alert on doors held or forced open.
* Review hinge exposure, glazed panels beside locks, and ceiling voids above partition walls as alternative routes.
* Include hardware bypass in physical testing, since it is invisible to an audit of the access control software.
data.short_recommendation: Fit door hardware that resists latch and sensor attacks.
